nameStory: The Arctic Hiatella gets its name from its ability to thrive in the frigid waters of the Arctic Ocean, though it's found in oceans worldwide. The genus name 'Hiatella' comes from the Latin word for 'gaping,' referring to how these clams can't completely close their shells. It's also called the 'wrinkled rock-borer' because of its corrugated shell surface and impressive ability to drill holes into soft rock.
description: The Arctic Hiatella is a hardy saltwater clam that's built like a tiny bulldozer. Its thick, white shell is roughly rectangular but wonderfully irregular in shape, almost like it's been hand-sculpted by ocean currents. These tough little mollusks grow up to about 1.8 inches long and are masters of making themselves at home in the most challenging rocky environments. Unlike many clams that burrow in sand, these adventurous bivalves prefer to attach themselves to hard surfaces or even bore right into soft rocks.

idTips.label: Shell Shape
idTips.description: Look for a thick, white shell that's roughly rectangular but distinctly irregular and lumpy, like a weathered stone that's been tumbled by waves

idTips.label: Shell Texture
idTips.description: Feel the surface - it's notably wrinkled and corrugated with deep ridges that catch your fingernail when you run it across

idTips.label: Shell Closure
idTips.description: Notice that the shell never closes completely tight - there's always a small gap visible even when the clam tries to shut

idTips.label: Attachment Method
idTips.description: Often found firmly attached to rocks or nestled deep in crevices, sometimes with visible brown, thread-like fibers (byssus) anchoring it

idTips.label: Size Range
idTips.description: Typically ranges from thumbnail-sized juveniles to mature adults about the length of your thumb

habitat: In New England waters, you'll find Arctic Hiatella clams clinging to rocky shores from the low tide line down to deeper waters. Look for them wedged into rock crevices, attached to pier pilings, or nestled among mussel beds along the Maine coast and other rocky shorelines. They're particularly fond of hiding among kelp holdfasts and in the nooks and crannies of granite ledges where waves crash.

seasonality.spring: Best time for shore exploration as winter storms have passed but summer crowds haven't arrived. Look for specimens newly exposed by storm action in rock crevices.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for low-tide exploration when you can access more of their rocky habitat. They may be more active and easier to spot during warm months.
seasonality.fall: Still accessible during calm weather, though shells may show more wear from summer wave action. Good time to find specimens before winter storms.
seasonality.winter: Difficult to observe due to harsh conditions and limited safe shore access, though the clams remain active in deeper waters below the ice.

funFact: These remarkable clams are basically living drills - they can actually bore holes into solid limestone and other soft rocks by constantly rotating their shells and secreting acids, creating perfectly fitted homes that protect them from predators and waves!
confusionNotes: Arctic Hiatella can be confused with young mussels, but remember that mussels have smooth, dark shells that close tightly, while these clams have wrinkled white shells that always gape open. Think 'Wrinkled and White with a Wide gap' for Hiatella versus 'Smooth and Shut' for mussels.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'Arctic' Hiatella, don't let the name fool you - these adaptable clams live in oceans from the poles to the tropics, making them one of the most widespread bivalves on Earth. The 'arctic' name simply reflects where scientists first extensively studied them.
compareHints: Since Arctic Hiatella is the only species in its genus found in New England, compare it to other rock-dwelling bivalves in the region. Unlike the smooth, elongated shells of razor clams or the fan-shaped shells of scallops, Hiatella has that distinctive chunky, rectangular profile with deep wrinkles. Its thick, irregular shell sets it apart from the more symmetrical shapes of most other local clams.
